cells.tense: You're moving first and holding the weight that comes with it, and both are yours.
cells.ask: offer to stay curious about one thing you could just as easily command — let it teach you something you didn't know
cells.core:
When you're carrying something that has to hold, you lead it — you step out front and take the weight and the two don't fight each other. You've stopped pushing at the load to prove you can bear it, and that's why people follow you into hard things — not because you're loud, but because you've already stood where they're being asked to stand.

You're the one going first here, and you own it. Under all that holding, you can also stop to look — the leader who stays curious is the one still standing after the push has passed. That curiosity is what's free to feed next, and it doesn't weaken the line you set. It makes the line worth holding.
cells.sheetLine: You lead and you carry, and you know both are yours.
cells.verb: leading from the front and setting the line by crossing it
cells.place: where you hold what has to be held

cells.tense: You're bracing for a fight that's already running, and you're already pushing before anything's landed.
cells.ask: step back far enough to see the shape of the whole thing before you move — see the pattern first, then go
cells.core:
You're charging ahead of the moment. There's a picture of how this has to go sitting out in front of you, and you're spending your strength getting there before it's time. The pushing is starting to cost you the ground it was meant to take.

When you're holding well, you lead from the front and things make sense around you. Nothing demands to be forced when it's going right. What gets you back isn't more force — it's taking the step back that lets you see the shape of the whole thing before you leap. That pause isn't retreat. It's what makes the move count.
cells.sheetLine: You're pushing ground you haven't reached yet.
cells.verb: leading from the front and setting the line by crossing it
cells.place: where you hold what has to be held

cells.tense: You set the line and you're still standing on the far side of it, not moving.
cells.ask: steady one small structural change into the ground this week — slow and persistent, not loud — and let that be enough
cells.core:
There was a line you were going to set. The deciding stopped and the standing still took over. You still carry what's around you, but you've gone quiet about the leading — and the carrying alone isn't the same as the move you were going to make.

Held right, this is the ground that keeps other people standing — you take the weight and they get to build on it. What gets you back isn't finding the nerve to charge. It's letting one real change come through you slowly and persist — the kind that keeps going after the moment passes. That's how the front gets crossed from where you're standing.
cells.sheetLine: You're carrying without moving, and it's starting to look the same.
cells.verb: leading from the front and setting the line by crossing it
cells.place: where you hold what has to be held

cells.tense: You're already steering this — you're the one holding it together — but you talk about it like it's just what happened.
cells.ask: say out loud one ending you're actually carrying, and what you're making room for by holding it
cells.core:
You're the one keeping this upright. The decisions are coming through you, the ground is holding because you're holding it — and you describe it as if it's just how things are. The leading is happening. The owning of it isn't.

When you do own it, it looks like knowing what to keep and what to let fall — clear and reliable, so things make sense in your presence. The move back is to name one ending you've been carrying quietly: what you're letting go of, and what you're making room for by holding what you hold. That claim is yours to make, and all it takes is saying it.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one carrying it, and it's yours to name.
